alcyoneus: Alcyoneus is among the greatest of the Giants, and immortal for as long as he fights on the ground where he was born. Heracles has to drag him out of his own country to kill him.
amazimu: Amazimu are cannibal ogres of Zulu and wider Nguni tradition: large, dangerous, and consistently defeated by children who pay attention.
antaeus: Antaeus, son of Poseidon and Gaia, wrestles every traveller who crosses his country in Libya, kills them all, and roofs a temple to his father with their skulls. He cannot lose while he is touching the ground.
balor: Balor of the Evil Eye leads the Fomorians. His single eye is kept shut and needs four men to lift the lid, and whatever it looks at dies.
baqbaq-devi: Cut off a devi's head and another grows. So the hero did not bring a sword.
bendigeidfran: His head is buried under London, facing France, still on duty.
bestla: Bestla is a giantess, daughter of the jötunn Bölthorn, and the mother of Odin. The gods who kill Ymir and build the world from him are themselves half giant, and Bestla is the half.
briareus: Briareus has a hundred hands and fifty heads. He is not an enemy of the gods but the reason they hold power, and Zeus keeps him in reserve as a threat that never has to be used twice.
british-giants-lesser: Britain kept more giants than it had room to remember properly. These are the ones who left a name and not much else.
cormoran: Cormoran is the giant of St Michael's Mount who waded ashore to steal Cornish cattle. Jack dug a pit, covered it, blew a horn at dawn, and the giant walked into it: the first kill in a career that gave English a phrase.
croatian-giants-lesser: Four smaller Croatian traditions, each too thin to stand alone and too specific to lose.
daidarabotchi: Mount Fuji is the soil he dug out of one province. Lake Biwa is the hole he left in another.
dragonja: He dragged a plough from the mountains to the sea. Water followed the furrow, and he named it Mirna.
dzunukwa: Dzunukwa is the wild woman of the woods in Kwakwaka'wakw tradition: enormous, dark, drowsy, with pursed lips and a basket for carrying children. She is also a source of wealth, and both facts matter equally.
enceladus: Enceladus is one of the Giants who rose against the Olympians and lost. He is buried under Sicily, and Mount Etna is what he does about it.
fangfeng: Fangfeng arrived late to Yu the Great's assembly of the lords and was executed for it. Centuries later a cartload of enormous bones was dug up, and Confucius was asked to identify them.
gaoh: Gaoh is the master of the winds in Haudenosaunee tradition, keeping the four directional winds in his charge. Each wind has its animal, and what the weather does depends on which one he releases.
gargantua: Rabelais did not invent him. The name was already in use as a nickname in 1470, and by then the countryside was full of his furniture.
geryon: Geryon has three bodies joined at the waist, or three heads on one trunk, depending on who is describing him. He keeps a herd of red cattle on an island at the western edge of the world, and Heracles is sent to take them.
giant-of-kandahar: The Giant of Kandahar is a story that a US special forces team killed a red-haired, six-fingered giant in Afghanistan in 2002. There is no evidence for it, and the story's actual history is documentable.
giant-of-kunar: A parallel Afghanistan story places a giant in the Kunar valley. Like the Kandahar version, it has no verifiable source, and the two accounts have merged in circulation.
gigantes: The Greek giants may not have been giants. In the earliest art they are painted as ordinary armed men.
gogmagog: Gogmagog is the last giant of Albion, thrown off a Cornish cliff by the Trojan Corineus in a wrestling match. Two carved effigies of him and his conqueror have stood in the Guildhall of London for centuries.
hiranyakashipu: Hiranyakashipu wins a boon that makes his death nearly impossible, and the god he has forbidden finds the one gap in it. The story exists to demonstrate that a clever condition can always be met.
hrungnir: Hrungnir is the strongest of the giants, with a head and heart of stone and a shield and hone-stone for weapons. He is killed in the only formal duel Thor ever fights.
ispolini: God made three attempts at people, and the dwarves were too small to survive. The ispolini were the correction.
kahui-tipua: The Kāhui Tipua are a band of supernatural giants in southern Māori tradition, credited with shaping parts of the South Island landscape: including, in some accounts, the excavation of the great lakes.
kalev-kalevipoeg: In Estonian, the word kalev simply means giant. His wife's tears became the lakes.
katallani: One eye, and no knees. He ate people, but he could not bend his legs to chase them.
kee-wakw: The Kee-wakw is a cannibal giant of Abenaki and wider Wabanaki tradition: a being of winter, hunger and the frozen forest, whose appetite grows the more it eats.
klek: Seen from Ogulin, the mountain is a sleeping man. The peak is his head.
koljo: A giant who survives mostly as place-names, and a scholarly argument about whether he was ever a giant at all.
kua-fu: Kua Fu decides to race the sun. He runs it down across the sky, drinks the Yellow River and the Wei dry, dies of thirst on the way to the northern lakes, and his staff becomes a forest of peach trees.
kumbhakarna: Kumbhakarna, brother of Ravana, sleeps six months at a time. He meant to ask for the seat of Indra and asked for sleep instead, and the mistake defines him.
maero: Maero are wild forest beings of Maori tradition: hairy, with long bony fingers ending in claws, living apart in the bush and hostile to people who enter it.
mahabali: Mahabali is a demon king who ruled so well that the gods removed him for it. Every year at Onam, Kerala keeps the promise that lets him come back and look at what he built.
mapinguari: One eye. And a mouth that opens vertically, from the nose down to the stomach.
milzinai: In local legend they are the ancestors and they are respected. In fairy tales the same beings are monsters to be beaten.
mouros: They raised the standing stones in a single night, and their name may mean the dead.
nawao: The Nawao are described in some Māori traditions as a wild, strong people of the interior forests: sometimes framed as an earlier group overcome or absorbed in ancestral history. Accounts vary, and colonial-era writing distorted them badly.
nemri: They are called the old people. They could not die a natural death.
og-of-bashan: Og, king of Bashan, is the last survivor of the Rephaim. Deuteronomy offers his iron bed as proof of his size, and notes that it can still be seen in Rabbah: a footnote that turns a king into an exhibit.
ojancanu: The ojáncanu is a roughly ten-foot, one-eyed giant of Cantabrian mythology: red-bearded, forest-dwelling, destructive to livestock and people, often given extra fingers as a mark of excess. His female counterpart, the ojáncana, is sometimes fiercer still.
olentzero: Olentzero is the last of the Jentilak. He stayed when the other giants fled, and he now comes down from the mountains at midwinter with charcoal on his face and presents for children.
orion: Orion is a giant hunter of enormous size who walks through the sea with his head above the water. He is blinded, healed, killed, and finally set among the stars, where he is still hunting.
papinijuwari: The Papinijuwari are one-eyed giants of Tiwi tradition who hunt the sick and drink blood. They belong to a living island cosmology, and what is publicly known about them is a fraction of what exists.
patagonian-giants: Fifteen feet in 1520. Four inches taller than a sailor in 1773.
paul-bunyan: Paul Bunyan is a giant lumberjack with a blue ox named Babe. He is the best-known giant in American folklore and substantially an advertising creation, which is the most interesting thing about him.
polybotes: Polybotes is the Giant who ran from Poseidon. He was pursued across the Aegean, and the piece of Kos that was thrown after him is the island of Nisyros, which is still sitting on him.
porphyrion: Porphyrion is the king of the Giants in most accounts of the war against the gods. He is destroyed at the moment he is most nearly victorious, and by desire rather than by force.
quinametzin: The Quinametzin are the giants of central Mexican tradition who inhabited an earlier world-age and built the great structures the Aztecs found already standing. Teotihuacan and Cholula were attributed to them.
rubezahl: Rübezahl is the weather-spirit of the Krkonoše mountains on the Czech-Polish border. He rewards the honest, punishes the arrogant, and takes violent offence at his own name.
santa-elena-giants: In 1553 a Spanish chronicler wrote down what the Manta people told him about the giants who landed on their coast. Four centuries later, someone worked out what the bones were.
shuten-doji: Shuten-doji is the oni chief of Mount Oe who took women from Kyoto and ate them. He was killed by warriors who arrived disguised as mountain priests and poisoned him at his own banquet.
skrymir: Skrymir is the giant so large that Thor and his companions sleep the night in his glove and take it for a hall. He is also not real, and finding that out is the humiliation at the centre of the story.
stallo: Stallo is the large, slow, dangerous being of Sámi tradition who hunts people across the winter landscape and is beaten by wit rather than strength. Circular stone foundations across northern Scandinavia are still called Stallo sites.
surtr: Where Ymir has an origin, Surtr has none. He is already there: a fire giant standing guard at the border of Muspellheim since before the ordered cosmos began, waiting for the day he leads the sons of Muspell against the gods and burns the nine worlds to ash.
suur-toll: He was king of the island. He lived as a farmer.
svyatogor: Svyatogor is so strong that the earth cannot carry him, so he lives in the mountains and never comes down. His story is about strength that has nowhere to go.
talos: Talos is a giant of bronze who walks the coast of Crete three times a day and throws rocks at approaching ships. He was not born.
thrym: Thrym, lord of the jötnar, steals Thor's hammer and buries it eight leagues deep. His price for returning it is Freyja as his bride, and the story of how the gods answer is the funniest poem in the Edda.
tityus: Tityus assaulted Leto and was killed for it. His punishment is to lie stretched across nine acres of the underworld while two vultures eat his liver, which grows back.
tombe-dei-giganti: Around eight hundred of them across the island. They are called giants' tombs because nothing else seemed large enough to need one.
troll-iceland: Half the strange rocks in Iceland are trolls who misjudged the sunrise.
uriasi: The Danube came up to their ankles. They could reach the handles of the sky.
waligora-wyrwidab: Almost every giant in this catalogue is something to be survived. These two are the heroes.
xelhua: Xelhua is one of the giants who survived the flood, and he built the Great Pyramid of Cholula to reach the sky. The gods stopped him, which is the part of the story that has caused all the argument.
ysbaddaden: His eyelids were too heavy to lift on their own. Servants held them open with forks.
